Into the Shimmer BY JOE FORDHAM T - he book Annihilation - first in a trilogy by novelist Jeff VanderMeer - represented a style of speculative fiction loosely categorized as 'New Weird,' a genre that delves into humanity's relationship with technology and nature, with a twist of Lovecraftian horror. VanderMeer described his story - about the efforts of a clandestine organization, the Southern Reach, to investigate an alien presence in an unspecified North American swampland — as an exploration of 'the pervasive non-reality of our reality' and 'the relationship of landscape to individuals.' Filmmaker Alex Garland, a former novelist and screenwriter, was completing his feature film directorial debut, Ex Machina, when he accepted the challenge of adapting Annihilation for Skydance Media and Paramount Pictures. "The story was strange and original," observed Garland, iand the atmosphere was powerful. With any adaptation, you have to ask yourself, 'What is it that struck me?' For me, this was about atmosphere. I wanted to capture the feeling I experienced while reading, and everything flowed from that The screenplay depicted biologist Lena (Natalie Portman), who is shocked when her 1 / 28 missing soldier husband, Kane (Oscar Isaac), reappears without warning after a yearlong

ANNIHILATION absence on a covert government mission. When Kane quickly succumbs to seizures, authorities swoop in and Lena is brought before psychologist Doctor Ventress (Jennifer Jason Leigh) at the Southern Reach. Lena joins Ventress' four-woman science team, seeking answers to her husband's disappearance into Area X, a subtropical wilderness where an alien infestation is slowly encroaching behind an amorphous, reality-shifting barrier, the 'Shimmer.' One of the first to receive the screenplay was Garland's key Ex Machina collaborator at DNEG. 'Alex sent me his script while I was in the Alps shooting second unit on Spectre," recalled visual effects supervisor Andrew Whitehurst. "I was shooting Bond during the day and reading the screenplay by night. That started our conversations over the next year, during which we talked periodically. I did a few sketches to clarify ideas in my own mind, and I shared those with Alex. At the beginning of preproduction, we met at DNEG and brought our concept artists on board. We focused on designs that defined the look of the film, to help everybody get an idea of our goals so we could work out practical onset elements and how they'd integrate with CG. We knew there was going to be a lot of collaboration between the practical and special effects, stunts and art department, and we knew we'd have to hit the ground running. We had a little bit more time for the shoot than we had on Ex Machina - ten weeks - but there were a lot of different locations, and we all had to plan as thoroughly as possible." Other returning Ex Machina veterans included production designer Mark Digby, cinematographer Rob Hardy and creature effects supervisor Tristan Versluis. Visual effects 2 / 28 producer Roma O'Connor joined the team with stunt coordinator Jo McLaren and special

effects supervisor Hayley Williams. "It was a new experience for me to join discussions in an early concept stage," commented Williams. "Alex didn't want to assume what we could or couldn't do. He was up for discussing how we should approach each sequence to make the best use of visual effects versus special effects, brainstorming with all heads of department. We all knew, budget-wise, there was no point in creating in-camera effects that would be replaced. On the flip side of that, Andrew and his visual effects team had so much to do, it was great for me to join the discussion early to suggest how special effects could help." A major logistical consideration was the story's main location of Area X, a dreamlike wilderness partially inspired by Saint Mark's National Wildlife Refuge in Florida. "I'm always careful of what I suggest for shooting on location. Shooting out in a forest, I knew we'd be battling wind, rain and all the elements. I had to take all those factors into consideration and make sure Alex and his director of photography were aware of what we would be up against." T ment gathered reference imagery of U.S. forests and marshlands that were representative of Area X, and planned how to manipulate locations. "We had to make the U.K. look and feel like Mississippi, Florida, or wherever Area X was supposed to beii said Andrew Whitehurst.iThe art department planned to build trees out of fiberglass to a certain height, and visual effects would top them up. There was a lot of back and forth, reviewing what ANNIHILATION the production nevertheless elected to shoot with principal performers entirely on woodland locations around the production base in England, combined with studio work at Pinewood Studios for Southern Reach interiors. The art depart3 / 28

ANNIHILATION they could do, and what we could do to help, making sure that we got the maximum bang per buck on screen in every location." The strange flora of Area X, suggesting pristine nature under alien influence, involved set dressing into the natural vegetation of Windsor Great Park, in Oxfordshire, creating the illusion of fungal growths and outcroppings of exotic flowers. DNEG added tree canopies, extra lichens, and other growths to complement set dressings, and extended tree lines with Floridian trees and moss. Milk VFX, Nvizible and Union VFX added environmental features, such as subtle animated detailing of tumorous fungal growths. "We used a mixture of 3D and matte painting to bring 'tumors' to life," related Milk VFX visual effects supervisor Sara Bennett. ¿Alex wanted them to feel like they were breathing. It was a simple, almost imperceptible effect so viewers would register a little bit of weirdness. Milk VFX added mutant flora using digital paint and animation in Maxon Cinema 4D.iThey gave us reference pictures of flowers from Fukushima as a design guide in keeping with the visual theme of Area X. That included giant, weird-shaped yellow and white daisies, but with elongated and triangular heads. Our matte painting department created those effects, bringing plant life a little bit of movement, selectively adding foliage and creepersi For on-set atmospherics, Hayley Williams' special effects team ran hundreds of meters of lay-flat tubing through trees to pump in mist and fog. DNEG 2D lead Tom Rolfe added to the alien ambience, creating refractive light effects caused by the omnipresent Shimmer. "Inside Area X," explained Andrew Whitehurst, "the Shimmer had an iridescent 4 / 28 quality. We explored that during preproduction by joining a camera test day where we

asked everybody to bring in optically interesting objects. I had a crystal ball and some other items at home. Andy Lowe, our gaffer, had some theatrical lanterns, and we got hold of some old lenses and shone lights through those to create flares. We filmed hours of footage, picked the best bits and scanned those. Wherever Rob and Andy placed lights in the forest to create strange atmospheres, we dressed in our optical elements in 2D. We added rainbow patterns to specular reflections on water, similar to when jet contrails are backlit and refract with rainbow qualities. As the characters go deeper into the Shimmer, we ramped up those effects. We didn't want to detract from the performances, so it had to be a subliminal effect; and then, for certain key moments, we'd bring it front and center." differences between a book and a film," observed Alex Garland, "is that descriptive passages in a book rely on the imagination of the reader to visualize them. In film, we had to visualize the book's ideas, and we had a lot of conversations about how to visualize the concept of this alien. For it to feel truly alien, we had to decide what that alien looked like, why did it look like that, and - a term that Andrew and I talked about a lot - what was the 'clock speed' of the alien's thought processes? If this alien had traveled all the way across space, 300,000 years or longer, did it think at the same speed as a human? From those abstract conversations, we moved toward a visual. Andrew and I shared a ANNIHILATION xterior views of the Shimmer - seen from the Southern Reach as a diaphanous membrane engulfing the forest - took inspiration from screenplay descriptions that suggested a physical manifestation of the alien presence.iOne of the big 5 / 28

ANNIHILATION lot of common interests and we gravitated toward mathematics. The 3D representation of Mandelbrot fractals, making shapes that were born from Mandelbulbs, was key to unlocking our ideas." DNEG visual effects art director Jonathan Opgenhaffen developed conceptual paintings of Shimmer exteriors. "In Alex's screenplay," recalled Andrew Whitehurst, "the Shimmer was described as having a membranous quality with a liminal point that the characters passed through. It had to feel almost like a trick of the light, not solid light passing through a liquid surface. It was ever-expanding, ever-shifting, and ever-changing. We tried a lot of approaches in concept paintings, and Jonathan Opgenhaffen did some stellar work. We looked at photographic treatments, and J.M.W. Turner paintings - particularly his abstract treatments of nature, taking inspiration from the colors that he used as washes in his oil paints." DNEG CG supervisor Daniel Paulsson incorporated cascading 3D fractal forms in Side Effects Houdini into Shimmer manifestations that suggested the alien organism at its core. iWe took Mandelbulb geometry, rendered that, unwrapped it into a flat surface, and used that to push iridescence and refraction over background plates. We then layered multiple versions so it had an appearance of chaos; but it was mathematically and procedurally driven, and within that chaos there were patterns that foreshadowed the alien that we revealed later in the storyi The Shimmer has a disruptive influence on creatures that Lena and members of Ventress' team encounter as they move deeper into Area X. 'The creatures all represented slightly different things," noted Alex Garland. "Everything is cross-related, and 6 / 28 everything had to work according to our thematic story logic. The idea is that everything

ANNIHILATION in Area X is colliding - there are collisions of psychology and species, emotions and species, species and plants, mineral and tree forms - everything is formed from some collision, or multiple collisions." Area X creatures were realized through a fusion of effects methodologies, including practical prosthetics and animatronics. "Very early on," commented prosthetics and animatronics supervisor Tristan Versluis, "Alex had strong visuals in mind. He'd sketch and translate his ideas very well but, at the same time, he was open to any ideas we offered. In our brainstorm sessions, Alex explained how he wanted the film to move from suburbia to psychedelia, leading people into a world that was slowly changing and unfolding. With that in mind, our task was to build physical parts for encounters with creatures, fusing elements of animals, plants and humans as they merged into a species. Understanding that theme guided all of our designs to create this world where living organisms were slowly becoming something that we've never seeni Versluis and his team created animatronic and prosthetic pieces designed to work in concert with DNEG's CG creations, and assisted development of art department set dressings of Lena's biological findings. "The environment is her microscope," Versluis explained. "As Lena travels through Area X, she examines flowers and animals in the environment. Everything comes under scrutiny because the characters start to wonder what is real and what is not, and they question their own mental state. It becomes this paranoid world. I worked closely with the art department and production design in terms of materials. We discussed using silicones, latexes and different textures, especially in the 7 / 28 creation of fungus and lichen growths that they created as set dressings. There were con-

stant discussions: "This material does this; it does that. What can we do with it?"" B confusion is indicated in flash cuts to the formation of the phenomenon when a meteor falls to Earth, striking a lighthouse on a beach. DNEG created digital matte paintings for views of the meteorite in Earth orbit and its impact with the lighthouse. "As the meteorite strikes the lighthouse," explained Andrew Whitehurst, "we see some Shimmer begin to emerge. That was shot on location in Holkham, Norfolk, where the art department built a small section of the lighthouse wall and door. DNEG CG sequence supervisor Michael Smith-Kennard then added the rest of the lighthouse. Further fragmentary images end on a closeup of cellular mitosis - a video projection in Lena's university biology class. DNEG generated the cellular imagery as digital animation, as well as later scenes depicting Lena's microscopy of much stranger cell samples gathered in Area X. "All of the microscope images were digital," said Whitehurst. ¿We used reference of electron microscope images and other visualization systems of cells, which were helpful for animation timings. Lena's university projection was based on a cervical HeLa celli Lena's suburban home life in Baltimore, where her husband Kane unexpectedly returns, featured a partial set built in the U.K., which Union VFX adapted into an exterior view. "We started with footage and lidar data of the set," related Union VFX supervisor ANNIHILATION eginning in flashback, Lena is introduced in an interrogation cell where a Southern Reach official, Lomax (Benedict Wong), dressed in a medical containment suit, demands explanations for her recent emergence from Area X. Lena's 8 / 28

ANNIHILATION Simon Hughes. There was hardly any useable architecture in the plate, so we had to generate the house exterior by sourcing our own material to create a suburban town. One of our artists happened to be visiting his family in the States, and he photographed a lot of architecture that had a suburban look. The shot needed a little bit of a camera move to give it some dynamics, so we ended up doing a CG build of the house, trees, background buildings, and flowerbeds in the foreground. The shot ended up entirely generated, using our own photographic material and CG builds of the set as a structural guide. Authorities swoop in to seize Kane and subdue Lena, who reawakens at a Southern Reach encampment bordering the Shimmer. Mark Digby and supervising art director Denis Schnegg designed the Southern Reach set on the backlot at Pinewood. ¿They wanted the facility to feel like it was built out of modular prefabricated sections," said Andrew Whitehurst.iWe looked at a lot of Arctic research stations where they helicopter in parts and slot them together to survive extreme conditions. We filmed those interiors at Pinewood, and then DNEG added exteriors. Lena views the Shimmer from a Southern Reach balcony, then retreats to Ventress' office where oily, shifting Shimmer light permeates through windows. When we shot the office scene," Whitehurst recalled, "we hadn't finalized the look of the Shimmer. But I discussed the lighting with Rob Hardy and Andy Lowe, and we felt that because we were shooting in a confined set, we needed an exterior light source that had inherent drama, so we hung white silks outside the windows, fired light into those, and accented that with some directional warm light. That gave us a basis for whatever the Shimmer ended 9 / 28 up being." DNEG compositors used lumakeying and rotoscoping to integrate Shimmer

ANNIHILATION effects into the scene.There was a lot of shadow in the office, so if we had used greenscreen and de-spilled the image, we would have killed the plate. White silks not only helped our lumakeys, they acted as a giant bounce-card, and gave us ambient light washing into the room." For scenes of Ventress, Lena and other expedition members heading into the Shimmer, the filmmakers positioned white silk backings behind trees on location in Windsor. DNEG lead 2D artist Michael Kennedy integrated Shimmer effects behind branches.iWe created Shimmer animation by changing the parameters of the Mandelbulb equation said Whitehurst. A lot of artistic compositing work went into that. We did many versions before we nailed the look. The Shimmer was elusive. It had to be tangible enough to have a presence, but we did not want it to be obvious how we had achieved it." Shimmer compositions focused on characters.iMost of the time, Alex framed actors approaching the Shimmer so we'd feel its scale in relation to them. We restricted ourselves to the height of a camera mounted on a crane on the locationi After slipping through the Shimmer, team members become disoriented, lose contact with civilization, and chance upon a shack overgrown with flora, half-sunk into a swamp. The art department supplied set dressing around Wood Pond in Windsor, including partial dummy tree trunks. DNEG generated environmental composites and enhanced in-camera forest atmospherics. Union VFX augmented profusions of white orchids and veronica flowers with color treatments and mossy growths. Natalie Portman held real orchids on set," noted Simon Hughes. "We removed those and replaced them with CG 10 / 28 versions, with added color. We did rotomation of Natalie's fingers to drive interactions

with petals, and then ran extra simulations to create external wobble and flutter. We rendered petals in Arnold, and spent a lot of time working out their transparency and properties. We built five versions of veronicas and orchids, and added those to the set-dressed flowers, covering about 30 percent of the flowers in the plates. In wide shots, we used a combination of CG flowers and color correction on practical flowers that were further from camera." T the attack using stunts, mechanical effects and CG animation. ¿Tristan Versluis's creature effects team built a full-sized gator and sections of the animal for the cast to interact with," explained Andrew Whitehurst. The mutant alligator design first took shape as a clay maquette and then as a fullscale sculpture. "We based the creature design on a real creature," said Tristan Versluis. "We found photo reference of an albino alligator with very rare white pigmentation in Miami-Dade Zoological Park in Florida. We had to indicate genetic changes that were happening in Area X, so we sculpted mutations on the inside of the creature's mouth, giving it shark's teeth growing alongside alligator teeth. We built a full-size silicone dummy alligator for actors to interact with, as well as a closeup head with a fully-operational jaw that the characters could hold open while Natalie stuck her head inside. Hayley Williams' effects team dressed a full-scale buck to a rig that was dragged into ANNIHILATION he idyllic atmosphere is shattered when a violent force grabs physicist Josie Radek (Tessa Thompson), wrenches her back into the shack, and thrashes her inside. A giant albino alligator then explodes into view. The filmmakers staged I1 / 28

ANNIHILATION the water to create interactions on an object that was approximately the correct shape and color of the CG-animated alligator.iI worked alongside the art and marine departments on location," recalled Hayley Williams. "Construction built the hut so that it was half sunk. And then, to show interactions of the alligator launching out into the lake, the marine department excavated the floor of the lake. The alligator then had to launch at the women on the bank, where the water was about three feet deep. We submerged our rig below the surface." To establish the alligator's presence in the hut, the stunt department rigged a ratchet-pull to tug Radek backward, and the special effects team simulated a violent attack. "Alex wanted the audience to know that there was something huge and scary in there," said Williams. "We had to suggest something battering around inside the shack, which was supposed to be made of corrugated metal. We vacuum-cast lightweight panels that fitted onto the shed, and we fitted impact rigs inside, which bashed against the side of the hut to make it look like the creature was thrashing around and denting the walls.i For the alligator reveal, Versluis' team provided a silicone casting of the alligator form, which special effects molded in fiberglass and articulated. We put a full-size alligator buck on a skate," said Williams. "We moved that on a wire that ran down to pulleys fixed to one-meter-square metal plates that we sunk in the lake. We jointed the buck so when it splashed into the lake, it had a natural wiggle." For the alligator's re-emergence, the effects team built a three-stage, air-ram rig.iWe motivated that with air hoses that ran through the lake and went up and out across the bank to compressed air bottles. 12 / 28 When we launched the rig forward, it created a huge splash. A separate rig opened the

ANNIHILATION alligator's mouth. Once it reached a certain point, the mouth opened, it hit a step and the rig made it collapse back.i DNEG's Daniel Paulsson and Michael Smith-Kennard created a fully digital alligator with fleshy musculature and leathery reptilian skin simulations, which animation supervisor Jeremy Stewart animated and Tom Rolfe's 2D team integrated with in-camera effects, fluid simulations, and mud and vegetation interactions. For scenes of Lena using a machine gun to halt the creature's advance, special effects rigged in-camera pyrotechnics. "We molded the inside of the alligator's mouth cavity in soft materials," said Williams. "We added 30 pyrotechnic charges in the mouth. As Natalie opened fire, we let off all the pyro and sent blood and bits of alligator flying everywhere.i Ventress' team continues into Area X, where they briefly observe baby eels swimming in a pool. Milk VFX added translucent 'elvers' as an insert shot conceived in postproduction. "The elvers were an afterthought," said Sara Bennett. "They were based on a real eel, but we added tumors to them to tie into the idea of mutation that DNEG had established in its creature work. We modeled and rigged a dozen elvers and animated them procedurally, and then keyframed each eel to swim around and move in to nibble on something nondescript.i Later in the forest, Lena briefly observes a pair of delicate, albino deer, crested with floral growths on their antlers. "I designed the deer in my notebook while we were shooting," said Andrew Whitehurst. "I sketched it very quickly on one of our tech recces. Alex asked me to make the neck a bit longer. When we came to filming, I had a profile drawing 13 / 28 of the creature. We blew it up on a photocopier, stuck it to some plywood and placed it

into the environment for eyelines for Natalie. DNEG then fleshed out that design, built and rigged it, and made it beautifuli T VFX added surrounding terrain seen from a guard tower. "We filmed around a real guard tower on location," said Whitehurst. "That was in a precarious condition so we couldn't film at the top. The production built a version of the top of the guard tower on a soundstage. We added the environment behind that for a couple of daylight scenes and some night scenes, generating everything out of the window, and a couple of exterior shots." Within the base, Ventress' team discovers grisly evidence of a previous expedition, including video of Lena's husband who participates in field surgery on an unfortunate colleague, Meyer (Sammy Hayman), whose abdomen is infested with glassy eels. The creature effects team prepared prosthetics that allowed the scene to be captured in-camera, first using a pump-activated blood-knife effect on the performer, and then using prosthetics of Meyer's abdomen. "When the soldiers cut open his belly," explained Tristan Versluis, "they hold him down while he is seated shirtless in a chair. We knew that Alex wanted to capture as much in-camera as possible, so I asked if he could cast a slender actor and then we would build the actor's stomach out. We took a full upper-body cast and built a prosthetic chest and a stomach that was enlarged. Into that, we fitted silicone intestines that we slimed up and wrapped around the actor. The intestines went back ANNIHILATION he team arrives at the former Southern Reach outpost, which has been overgrown by vegetation. The production filmed principal performers among set dressing at an abandoned airbase in Upper Heyford, Oxfordshire. DNEG and Milk 14 / 28

ANNIHILATION through a fake wall, against which he was seated. We had our puppeteers behind the wall, pulling on the intestines, which slid around the actori DNEG provided digital rig clean-up and augmentation. Lightning in the Bottle BY JOE FORDHAM E Urnest Cline's literary debut, Ready Player One, presented a vision of a future where virtual reality, built on a framework of 1980s pop culture and computer games, served as a refuge for a disenfranchised population. The book made news when a publicity tie-in awarded a lucky reader with a DeLorean DMC-12 - the gull-winged sports car from Back to the Future, referenced in Cline's book. Warner Bros. snapped up movie rights, and shortly thereafter announced their next coup: who better to direct the adaptation than the producer of Back to the Future, Steven Spielberg? Legend spoke of Spielberg as an early tech adopter, who played the arcade game of Pong on the set of Jaws, and later equipped his Amblin Entertainment offices with his own personal cabinet consoles of Tetris, Donkey Kong and Space Invaders. Spielberg's films, heartfelt and diverse in subject matter, embraced innovation and his recent performance-capture-based animated films, The Adventures of Tintin and The BFG, set the stage for a journey into wilder virtual realms. As scripted by Cline and Zak Penn, Ready Player One straddled two worlds. The 1 / 36 first was the futuristic home of teenager Wade Watts (Tye Sheridan) in the slums of 2045

READY PLAYER ONE Columbus, Ohio. The second was Wade's existence in a multiplayer online game, or Ontologically Anthropocentric Sensory Immersive Simulation, the OASIS. While navigating the OASIS, Wade solves a puzzle bequeathed by recently-deceased OASIS-inventor James Halliday (Mark Rylance) and he obtains the first of three 'Easter egg' keys, which unlock Halliday's fortune and ownership of the OASIS. Placed at the top of the High Five of 'gunter' egg-hunters, Wade becomes arch enemy to Nolan Sorrento (Ben Mendelsohn), president of media conglomerate Innovative Online Industries, who seeks to corporatize the freedom of the virtual world.
